assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (magic-wavelength trapping, Katori's idea) combine Doppler- and recoil-free spectroscopy with thousands of atoms, giving fractional uncertainties at the 1e-18 level. This is a precision-instrument advance that opens new measurement regimes: relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, and a coming redefinition of the second. As an instrument builder I value the long calibration and systematics work behind it.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group brought it to the lowest systematic uncertainties and wide applications. A two-person prize is clean. Other strontium and ytterbium groups are not in the credited list, which is a mild fairness issue.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent laboratories worldwide; interpretation is stable and the technology is mature. Timely, with the SI redefinition of the second under discussion.
uncertainties: Part of the same lineage as the 2005 and 2012 prizes (frequency combs, trapped-ion control), so some members may see it as incremental.
Whether Ye's credit should be balanced against other clock pioneers is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The IceCube detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and later the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane associations, opened neutrino astronomy as a new observational window. It rests on a very large detector instrument built in Antarctic ice. This is squarely in my area and I consider it a major discovery.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube, so he is a defensible single laureate, but the discovery is the product of a large collaboration and the supplied credit is a single name. A fair configuration is difficult, and other leaders (for example in AMANDA, or on the analysis side) are not on the credited list, so I cannot propose a larger set from this entry.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is confirmed by multiple IceCube analyses and now supported by KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD hints. Source identification is still partial, but the discovery itself is established and about a decade old.
uncertainties: Single-name credit versus a collaboration-scale discovery.
The source associations are statistically moderate and the origin of the diffuse flux is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The measurement of the third neutrino mixing angle theta-13, which proved large enough to make CP violation in the lepton sector accessible, was a decisive reactor-antineutrino experiment. It required careful control of detector systematics via identical near and far detectors. This is a textbook case of a precision measurement that changed the field.
assessment.attribution: Daya Bay (Wang as spokesperson, Luk as US co-spokesperson) and RENO (Kim) announced in 2012. Double Chooz, which reported earlier hints, and T2K's electron-neutrino appearance evidence are not credited here. Three names are possible, but the allocation is contested and spokesperson roles do not equal individual credit.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by several independent experiments and stable. Recognition is timely, but the 2015 prize on neutrino oscillations may reduce appetite for a second neutrino-mixing prize.
uncertainties: Who made the decisive contribution among Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz is disputed.
Whether the committee views this as an extension of the 2015 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Baryon acoustic oscillations as a standard ruler give a geometric probe of expansion that is largely free of astrophysical systematics, and they now underpin dark-energy constraints from SDSS, BOSS and DESI. The prediction by Sunyaev and collaborators, followed by the 2005 detections, is a clean theory-to-measurement story with lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: The 2005 detection came from the SDSS luminous red galaxy sample (Eisenstein) and the 2dFGRS power spectrum (Cole, Percival). The theoretical origin (Sunyaev and Zeldovich, Peebles and Yu) is only partly represented, and I cannot add names beyond the credited strings. Choosing three observers over Sunyaev is a judgement; the alternative is to include Sunyaev, but that would break the three-person limit without dropping an observer.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations; the method is a cornerstone of precision cosmology. Mature, though the dark-energy interpretation from DESI is still evolving.
uncertainties: Fair split between theory origin and observational detection.
Recent DESI results hinting at evolving dark energy might change the physical interpretation, though not the BAO detection itself.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The ATLAS and CMS detectors were the instruments that made the 2012 Higgs discovery possible: huge multi-technology calorimeters, trackers and muon systems operating at unprecedented rates. As a detector builder I think instrument-level recognition is deserved, and the Higgs itself was prized in 2013.
assessment.attribution: These three led the early proposals and long construction phases (ATLAS spokesperson Jenni, CMS spokesperson Della Negra, CMS project leader Virdee). Thousands of others made decisive contributions, and the Nobel rules make any instrument prize look arbitrary compared with the collaboration. The credit is plausible but not obviously fair.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed by a decade of performance; timing is fine, but the 2013 Higgs prize makes a second LHC award a hard sell.
uncertainties: Whether the committee will recognise detector construction after already prizing the theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: WMAP produced the first full-sky, high-precision CMB maps and fixed the parameters of the Lambda-CDM model to percent level, with the age of the universe, the baryon and dark-matter densities and the reionisation epoch. Calibration, foreground treatment and systematics control are central, which I respect.
assessment.attribution: Bennett led the mission, Spergel led the cosmological interpretation and Page was a leading instrument and design scientist. This is a reasonable configuration, though Wilkinson, Wright and others contributed. COBE (2006) and Planck complicate the novelty claim.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed and extended by Planck and ACT/SPT. Very mature; the question is whether the incremental precision step merits a prize after COBE.
uncertainties: Overlap with the COBE prize and with Planck, which many see as the definitive successor.
Allocation among mission leadership, instrument and analysis roles.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision instrument for gravimetry, gradiometry, tests of the equivalence principle and measurement of the fine-structure constant. It is a direct instrument-development achievement with growing applications in navigation and fundamental physics.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard built the first atom interferometers and Kasevich brought them to precision gravity and inertial measurement, while Bordé developed the theory of atom-light interferometers. Chu, who has a prize, and Chu-related work, plus Cornell and Ketterle's condensates, overlap; this is a workable three-person set.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many laboratories and now being deployed in space and field settings. Fully mature, though the impact on fundamental physics is still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 laser cooling prize and the 2001 condensate prize.
Relative weight of Bordé's theoretical role.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The kilonova, the radioactively powered transient from r-process nucleosynthesis in a neutron-star merger, was predicted theoretically, then seen in GRB 130603B and decisively in AT2017gfo with GW170817. It links gravitational waves, gamma rays and heavy-element synthesis, and is a landmark of multi-messenger astronomy.
assessment.attribution: Metzger and Kasen developed the models; Tanvir reported the near-infrared kilonova counterpart to GRB 130603B. Many observers of AT2017gfo, plus Li and Paczynski who first proposed the idea, are not credited here, so the allocation is open.
assessment.maturity: GW170817 is one well-observed event with strong follow-up; further kilonovae are few. Confirmation is good but the sample is limited, and the 2017 prize already recognised gravitational waves.
uncertainties: Priority and credit are widely shared across theory and observation.
